comment: The authoritative list of E/F mutation correctness classes.
Totals are derived from this file, never from prose. A class is terminal
only when result is CAUGHT or TRUE_NO_OP and every dimension below holds:
Combined-bypass mutations carry a C suffix so they are never counted as
Each class declares, so that no future reviewer needs the conversation that
produced it: the file and anchor the mutation applies to, the permanent test
that asserts the fixture contains the attacked structure, the narrow probe
that shows the mutant expresses the intended defect, and the killer's argv
and expected tests. The harness fills in the evidence block from the runs.

classes.name: CreateMaterializedView keeps embedded indexes

expresses: CreateMaterializedView keeps the indexes its payload carried, so replaying a
migration adds each index twice: once from the relation operation and once
from the CreateIndex beside it.

note: The planner strips a relation operation's indexes before writing an
artifact, so no end-to-end fixture can reach this class. What it defends
against is an artifact the planner did not write — committed before that
was fixed, or edited by hand — which makes replay through the artifact
the only level at which the property is observable, and the killer.

expresses: CreateIndex.Apply appends the index to the relation's state twice, so one
CREATE INDEX in a migration leaves two logical entries behind. The
database only ever sees one statement, so no catalog assertion finds it;
what breaks is the next plan.
DropIndex.Apply removes the entry and appends it again, so the index
survives its own drop in replay state while PostgreSQL really loses it.
The state and the database then disagree in the direction no catalog
assertion looks at.
The matview index planner loses the branch that drops an index the
declarations do not have, so any extra state entry — a duplicate among
them — is treated as agreement and every plan comes out empty.
CreateIndex.Apply resolves tables only, so an index on a materialized view
cannot be placed when the migration that creates it is replayed.
DropIndex.Apply resolves tables only, so an index on a materialized view
cannot be found when the migration that drops it is replayed. CreateIndex
still resolves both, which is what makes this the DropIndex class.
An index-only change drops and recreates the materialized view instead of
planning the index operations, discarding every stored row to add an index.
sameIndex stops comparing uniqueness, so a unique index and a plain one over the same keys are the same object.
sameIndex sorts the key lists by name before comparing them, so (a, b) and (b, a) are the same index.
sameIndex stops comparing key direction, so ASC and DESC on the same key are the same index.
sameIndex stops comparing NULLS ordering, so NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST on the same key are the same index.
sameIndex exempts gin from the method comparison, so GIN metadata specifically becomes ineffective while other methods are still compared.

classes.name: GiST ignored

expresses: sameIndex stops comparing the access method whenever either side is gist,
so GiST metadata specifically becomes ineffective while every other
method is still compared. The other-method axes therefore stay green,
which is what makes this a GiST class rather than a method class.

note: The mutation attacks schema's index comparison, which is the drift
authority. migrate has its own copy for planning, so a planner killer
is green under this mutation and was the killer-execution failure the
first run reported. The killer is therefore the drift path, and the
authority test that pins the two copies together is recorded beside it.

expresses: sameIndex stops comparing the access method whenever either side is brin,
so BRIN metadata specifically becomes ineffective while every other
method is still compared.
sameIndex stops comparing the partial predicate, so two indexes over the same keys with different WHERE clauses are the same index.
sameIndex stops comparing INCLUDE, so a covering index and a plain one are the same object.

classes.name: expression key simplified

expresses: sameIndex stops comparing key expressions, so an index over lower(title) and one over a plain column are the same index.

note: The expression case in the axis table moves three slots, because an
expression key has no name and no operator class. It is therefore caught
by the key-name comparison whether or not expressions are compared, and
is not a valid killer for this class. The one-axis question is two
different expressions, which is TestSameIndex_expressionsAreCompared.
The fixture precondition records the three-slot count for the same reason.

expresses: sameIndex stops comparing operator classes, so text_pattern_ops and the default are the same index.
indexHolderOf resolves an index's owner by relation name alone, so the
schema an operation names is ignored and a namesake in another schema
can be selected instead.
Qualifies stops requiring uniqueness. Production can never supply a
non-unique candidate — they are built from the table's unique indexes —
so no fixture reaches it. 20C supplies one directly.
The same mutation, with a killer that supplies a non-unique candidate
directly instead of going through a production path that cannot. This is
what shows the rule is load-bearing rather than dead code.
A partial unique index qualifies for a concurrent refresh. It constrains only
the rows it covers, so PostgreSQL was always going to reject the REFRESH.
An expression unique index qualifies. It has no column list to match rows by,
so PostgreSQL was always going to reject the REFRESH.
An index whose keys mix a plain column and an expression is recorded as plain,
because the expression flag is only set when every key is one. It then
qualifies for a concurrent refresh the server will reject.
A unique index carrying INCLUDE columns is recorded as partial, so it stops
qualifying. INCLUDE columns are not part of the key and constrain nothing, so
such an index does cover every row and PostgreSQL accepts it. This is the
class in the opposite direction: a rule refusing what is valid.
The preflight stops requiring a qualifying index, so Refresh(Concurrently)
sends a statement the server was always going to reject — taking the lock it
was avoiding and letting the server do the refusing.

classes.name: CONCURRENTLY + WITH NO DATA guard removed

expresses: CONCURRENTLY combined with WITH NO DATA is accepted and sent. A concurrent
refresh replaces contents row by row and there are no rows to replace with.

classes.name: qualifying index omitted from MatView fingerprint

expresses: The qualifying index leaves the fingerprint material: the mapping digest
no longer varies with which index a concurrent refresh may use, so an
eligibility-changing migration moves nothing and the committed generated
descriptor is never reported stale.

classes.name: table indexes enter table fingerprint

expresses: An ordinary table's unique indexes are written into its fingerprint
material. A table's generated code does not depend on its indexes, so
every table-only project's lock moves on an index change that changed
nothing about what was generated.

note: The first killer was TestTableOnly_bytesAreStable, which compares two runs
of one project. Both runs carry the same leaked index metadata, so it is
green under the mutation. Byte stability across runs is a different
property from index metadata staying out of the fingerprint.

expresses: The call site restates the eligibility rule locally instead of passing its
candidates through the one package that owns it, and the restatement has
drifted: it forgets that an expression index has no column list to match rows
by. That is the shape the eligible package exists to make impossible.
Compare accepts a fingerprint that does not match the lock, so generated
code produced from a different mapping is reported as current.
A failed concurrent refresh returns the local preflight message instead of
the server's error, so PostgreSQL's refusal never reaches the caller and
errors.As finds no PgError under it.
Whether the materialized view currently holds data is written into the
portable mapping fingerprint, so an ordinary refresh reports committed
generated code as stale.
CheckMaterializedIndexes drops the findings that say an index is
only in the declarations, so a declared index the database does not
have is never reported. A changed index and a live index nobody
declared still are, which is what makes this the missing-index class
rather than index checking removed.
sameIndex stops comparing the partial predicate. #15 attacks the same comparison as declared metadata; this attacks it as drift against a live database.
sameIndex stops comparing the access method entirely, so every method is the same as every other.
sameIndex stops comparing uniqueness, attacked as drift: an index that lost its uniqueness by hand.
sameIndex stops comparing INCLUDE, attacked as drift: an index given a covering column by hand.
The chooser keeps whichever qualifying candidate arrived first. Unique
indexes are read with ORDER BY ic.relname, so they arrive lowest-name-first
and the first met is the lowest named: nothing end to end can observe it.
38C supplies them out of order directly.
The same mutation, with killers that supply the candidates out of name
order directly. #40 is the other half of this: the same chooser attacked
together with the catalog ordering that absorbs it.

classes.name: declaration order affects selection

expresses: Unique indexes are read in descending name order, so the model no longer
receives them lowest-name-first. This is the second of the two
independent ordering guarantees; on its own it is absorbed by the
chooser, which is why it is applied together with the site below.
The call site bypasses the canonical chooser and returns the first
qualifying candidate it meets, so selection follows the order the
declarations were written in rather than a stable rule.

note: Selection order is guaranteed twice: by ORDER BY ic.relname when the
catalog is read, and by the chooser taking the lowest qualifying name.
Either alone is sufficient, so a single-site mutation is absorbed and is
neither a survivor nor a no-op. The recorded mutation is the combined
bypass; the narrow probe beside it shows the single site really was
expressed.

classes.name: catalog order affects selection

expresses: Unique indexes are read in descending name order, so the model no longer
receives them lowest-name-first. This is the second of the two
independent ordering guarantees; on its own it is absorbed by the
chooser, which is why it is applied together with the site below.
The chooser keeps whichever qualifying candidate arrived first instead of
the lowest name, so the answer depends on the order a catalog or a
declaration happened to supply.

note: Selection order is guaranteed twice: by ORDER BY ic.relname when the
catalog is read, and by the chooser taking the lowest qualifying name.
Either alone is sufficient, so a single-site mutation is absorbed and is
neither a survivor nor a no-op. The recorded mutation is the combined
bypass; the narrow probe beside it shows the single site really was
expressed.

classes.name: PostgreSQL major enters fingerprint

expresses: The PostgreSQL major is read from the server during introspection and
carried into the model, so the portable fingerprint becomes a
statement about which major produced it.
What introspection recorded about the server it read reaches the portable
mapping digest. On its own this leaks only the configured search path,
which is a project fact; it is the capture site beside it that makes the
leaked value server-local.

note: The fingerprint's input carries no server major and no database name, so
there is no value in scope for a single-site mutation to leak. The class is
therefore expressed as the two steps a real defect would take: capture the
fact while a connection is in hand, then write it into the portable digest.

classes.name: database name enters fingerprint

expresses: The database name is read from the server during introspection and
carried into the model, so one project produces a different lock in
every database it is generated against.
What introspection recorded about the server it read reaches the portable
mapping digest. On its own this leaks only the configured search path,
which is a project fact; it is the capture site beside it that makes the
leaked value server-local.

note: The fingerprint's input carries no server major and no database name, so
there is no value in scope for a single-site mutation to leak. The class is
therefore expressed as the two steps a real defect would take: capture the
fact while a connection is in hand, then write it into the portable digest.

expresses: The relation's OID is written into the portable fingerprint. Two databases
built from one migration assign different OIDs, so one project produces
different locks on different servers.
The server's deparsed definition — ServerCanonical — is written into the
portable fingerprint, crossing the F0 boundary. PostgreSQL 16 stopped
qualifying columns it need not, so one unchanged declaration produces
different portable bytes on 14 and 16.

classes.name: Type discovery narrows back to table columns

expresses: Type discovery walks table columns only, while column resolution covers
every readable relation. A type that appears solely on a view or
materialized view column — count(*) is bigint in a schema that stores no
bigint — then resolves against a map that never loaded it, and
introspection fails with "has type OID 20, which was not loaded".

note: The killer is end to end because that is the level the defect was reported
at: a project generating against a database whose only bigint is a
count(*). The semantic pair is the same property at the introspector, on a
view and on a materialized view, because the defect was never specific to
materialized ones.
This class was added after the batches above and ran on its own, in an
isolated worktree checked out at 19158d9 - the commit that carries the fix,
the fixture and this entry. The manifest-level evidence_commit covers the
earlier batches and is left as it was, because rewriting it would claim they
were re-run when they were not.

evidence_commit_note: bddf3d6 is the revision the mutations were applied to and the killers run at,
in an isolated worktree checked out at exactly that commit.
Recording it here necessarily produces a later commit, because this file is in
the repository. That commit differs from bddf3d6 by this file alone — no Go
source, no test — so the code under test and the code at HEAD are the same.
An earlier pass recorded the commit before the one it ran against, which is the
same slip in the other direction and is why the rule is written down.
